catalog_quote: p.15: "4. ACCENT In order to obtain a good pronunciation of these languages, especially of Ndogo, great attention must be paid to the accent. The following suggestions (I shall not call them rules) may serve as a guide for Ndogo. I. No difficulty for monosyllables. II. In connection with polysyllables, attention must be paid to the fact that a good few of such words are compound ones, actually made up of two or more monosyllables, each one of which must have its own accent duly stressed. ... III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first. The latter are listed here as a guide to the reader: words having l r n in the second syllable. ... V. Bviri. Most of the remarks made for Ndogo hold good." p.29: "(d) As hinted above (5. iv.), the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables: thus, in reduplication, accents lie on the first and third syllables. Out of the numerous examples given above only mbulàmbulà makes an exception ..." p.8 (sec. 2 Vowels): "II. Bai ... This language wavers between Ndogo and Bviri. Generally speaking it follows closely the former."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level (Ndogo-modelled) accent sketch for the Ndogo-Sere-Tagbu-Bai-Bviri languages: monosyllables unproblematic; polysyllables are mostly compounds and each component keeps its own accent; in dissyllables the accent 'usually lies on the first syllable' (clearly so when the second syllable has l, r, n; other dissyllables have 'even stress' on both syllables); reduplicated dissyllables are accented on syllables 1 and 3. The languages are tonal (sec. 5, four pitch levels). Nothing is said about accent in Bai specifically; Bai is stated to follow Ndogo closely, and the Ndogo remarks are said to hold for Bviri.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such; compounds and reduplications carry an accent on each component (syllables 1 and 3 in reduplicated dissyllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Dissyllables without l/r/n in the second syllable have 'even stress on both syllables'; reduplication mbulambula accented on the second syllable of each component; predicative adjectives/verbs with lengthened final vowel take the 'accent on the doubled vowel' (p. 26); with r in the second syllable that syllable is often lost (mboro = mboo, koro = koo).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level pronunciation guidance for isolated words (author calls them 'suggestions', not rules), framed for the whole group with Ndogo as the model; Bai only covered by implication (p. 8 'follows closely' Ndogo). Text accessed as verbatim Google Books snippets, not continuous pages; remark V (Bviri) continuation and any further Bai detail not recovered.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted accent statement is a group-level sketch in a comparative grammar of Ndogo-Sere-Tagbu-Bai-Bviri, explicitly modelled on Ndogo (ndog1248) and explicitly extended to Bviri (Belanda Viri, bela1255); Bai (baii1251, bdj) is not named in the accent section and is covered only via p. 8 'This language wavers between Ndogo and Bviri. Generally speaking it follows closely the former.' Not to be confused with the Sino-Tibetan Bai of Yunnan (full-text hits for 'Bai language stress' are all that language).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Santandrea-1961-based reading 'tone language with a stress statement' (Ndogo accent usually on the first syllable of dissyllables; Bai follows Ndogo closely). Tucker & Bryan add the type-level detail (three-level tone system; stress conditions vowel quality/length; unstressed-syllable vowel reduction in Ndogo-Sere) but give no placement, so they neither confirm nor contradict the first-syllable tendency. Confidence medium: the item is lending-only and was read through search snippets, not a page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Sere-Mundu/Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi group (Ndogo-Sere = Santandrea's Ndogo, Bai, Bviri, Sere) is described as tonal with three level tones; stress is mentioned only as a conditioner of vowel quality and length (Ndogo-Sere vowels have reduced 'subsidiary' qualities in unstressed syllables), and no position for word stress is stated for Ndogo-Sere or for Bai. The one placement-like remark (penultimate vowel length in Mayogo; extra shortness there in Ngbaka, Gbaya, Banda) concerns other languages of the chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the chapter's stress paragraph is group-level and says nothing specific to Bai. Bai occurs in the chapter only in comparative tables (noun-plural prefix nda-, demonstratives 'BAI vi nu / vi na', pronouns); no sentence pairs BAI with stress/accent/penultimate anywhere in the item's scanned.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan treat Santandrea's Sudan cluster as a single unit 'NDOGO-SERE' (Ndogo, Bai, Bviri, Sere; Tagbu is absent from the item's scanned) inside a comparative chapter that also covers Mundu, Mayogo, Ngbaka Ma'bo, Ngbaka Gbaya, Banda/Togbo/Mbanja and Ngbandi; the sec. 2b remarks about penultimate length or shortness concern Mayogo, Ngbaka, Gbaya and Banda, not Bai. Bai data in the chapter come from Santandrea 1934 (A comparative grammar of Ndogo, Sere, Bai and Bviri) and his contributed sketches.
